items.stem: Examine any three effects of Print culture on the French Revolution.
items.answer: Print culture prepared the ground for the French Revolution in three main ways. (1) It made the wide circulation of ideas possible: people who disagreed with established authority could now print and circulate their views, and through the printed message they persuaded others to think differently. (2) It speeded up the mobilisation of the masses behind the political ideals of freedom, liberty and justice for which the revolutionaries were fighting. (3) It exposed the draconian decisions of the monarchy and the higher estates, which awakened ordinary people and drew them into the revolution.

items.stem: How had the printing press created a new culture of reading in Europe? Explain with examples.
items.answer: With the printing press a new wave of print culture began in Europe. (1) Low cost of production: printing cut the cost of books because the time and labour needed for each copy fell sharply, so multiple copies could be made easily and books flooded the market for an ever-growing readership. (2) Accessibility of books: reading had earlier been restricted to the elites, while common people lived in an oral culture of sacred texts read out, ballads recited and folk tales narrated; cheap books now reached them. Before print, books were both expensive and too few in number, but now they could reach far wider sections of people. (3) Rising literacy: through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries literacy rates rose across most of Europe as churches of different denominations set up schools in villages, carrying literacy to peasants and artisans. As literacy and schools spread, Europe saw a virtual reading mania.

items.stem: “Print culture created the conditions within which French Revolution occurred.” Support the statement with suitable arguments.
items.answer: Print culture did create the conditions in which the French Revolution took place. (1) Print popularised the ideas of the Enlightenment thinkers. (2) These writers attacked the sacred authority of the Church and the despotic power of the state, eroding the legitimacy of a social order founded on tradition; Voltaire and Rousseau were widely read. (3) All values, norms and institutions came to be re-evaluated and discussed by a public that was inquisitive, critical and rational, so new ideas of social revolution came into being. (4) By the 1780s literature mocked royalty and criticised its morality, which fed hostile sentiment against the monarch.

items.stem: “Colonial administrators found ‘vernacular’ novels a valuable source of information on native life and customs.” Prove the statement by giving three evidences.
items.answer: Vernacular novels were useful to the colonial administration because they told the British about the Indian society they had to govern, a society of many communities and castes. (1) New novels such as ‘Indirabai’ described domestic life, showing how people dressed and what their religious beliefs and practices were; some of these books were translated into English by British administrators or Christian missionaries. (2) As outsiders the British knew very little about life inside Indian households, and the new novels in Indian languages carried exactly such descriptions of domestic life. (3) They recorded how people dressed, their forms of religious worship, their beliefs and their practices, which gave administrators first-hand information on native life and customs.

items.stem: Discuss in brief the development of printing culture in China.
items.answer: Printing culture in China developed in stages. (1) In the beginning China used hand printing, in which paper was rubbed against the inked surface of woodblocks. (2) In the sixteenth century the volume of print increased because civil service aspirants needed a growing number of textbooks. (3) With the blooming of urban culture in the seventeenth century the use of printed material grew once again. (4) Later China gradually moved from hand printing to mechanical printing.

items.stem: What is a manuscript ? Why were they not used widely ?
items.answer: A manuscript is a book or document written by hand — the author's original handwritten or typed copy, not printed. In ancient India most books existed only in manuscript form. They were not used widely because: (1) they were limited in number, so they were not accessible to all literate people; (2) they were not easy to handle, and carrying a big volume or an epic from one place to another was very difficult; (3) every individual's style of writing differs and some hands were very untidy, which made manuscripts hard to read.

items.stem: How were the books prepared in India in different languages before used of modern printing press ?
items.answer: Before modern printing technology reached India, books in the various Indian languages were prepared by hand. (1) Palm leaves or handmade paper were used to write the manuscript of a book. (2) Wooden covers were tied or sewn with the pages of the manuscript, made of bhojpatra and bark. (3) Calligraphy was practised to produce further copies of a manuscript. (4) Pages were duly illustrated, as can be seen in a page from the Diwan of Hafiz of 1824. (5) This way of making and writing books continued unbroken and exclusive until print was introduced in the late nineteenth century.

items.stem: How did press play an important role in spreading modern Indian nationalism in the second half of the 19th century ?
items.answer: The press was central to the spread of modern Indian nationalism. (a) It was the chief means of awakening the dormant people of India. (b) A large number of nationalist newspapers appeared during the second half of the nineteenth century. (c) In their columns official policies were constantly criticised and the Indian point of view was put forward; people were asked to unite and work for national welfare, and ideas of self-government, democracy and industrialisation were popularised. (d) The press also allowed nationalist workers living in different parts of the country to exchange views with one another.

items.stem: Explain the attitude of the British Government towards the Indian Press in the 19th century. Explain the main reasons for such an attitude.
items.answer: The British Government's attitude towards the Indian Press was one of control. (1) Restrictions were imposed on the Indian Press up to 1835 by Charles Metcalfe. (2) The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 curbed the freedom of the Indian Press, particularly of Indian-language newspapers. (3) The Act was repealed in 1882. (4) After that the press enjoyed considerable freedom for about twenty-five years. (5) Following the Swadeshi and Boycott movement of 1905, repressive press laws were again introduced in 1908 and 1910. The main reason for this attitude was to check the rising tide of Indian nationalism and of anti-British feeling among Indians.

items.stem: How did Martin Luther's writings bring reforms in religious field? Explain.
items.answer: Martin Luther (1483–1546) was a German monk, priest and professor of theology who wrote the ‘Ninety Five Theses’ criticising many practices and rituals of the Roman Catholic Church. He taught that salvation is not earned by good deeds but received only as the free gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ as redeemer from sin. He believed in the infallibility of the Bible but challenged the authority of the Pope. Because his theses were printed and distributed widely in Germany — his translation of the New Testament sold 5000 copies within a few weeks — his ideas spread very fast. A National Church was established in Germany and prayers began to be held in German, which marked the beginning of the Reformation Movement in Europe.

items.stem: How did print culture affect women in the nineteenth century India ?
items.answer: Print culture changed the position of women considerably. (1) The lives and feelings of women began to be written about in particularly vivid and intense ways, and women's reading increased enormously in middle-class homes; liberal husbands and fathers began educating their womenfolk at home and sending them to school. (2) In East Bengal in the early nineteenth century Rashsundari Debi, a young married girl in a very orthodox household, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen and later wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban, published in 1876 — the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language; a large part of it was devoted to the education of women. In the early twentieth century journals written for, and sometimes edited by, women became extremely popular.

items.stem:
What were the chief characteristics of the earliest print culture in Japan ? Explain any five.
or
Explain any three important characteristics of the print culture in Japan.
items.answer: The earliest print culture of Japan had these features. (1) Buddhist monasteries from China introduced hand-printing technology into Japan. (2) The oldest Japanese book printed in AD 868 is the Buddhist Diamond Sutra. (3) In medieval Japan poets and prose writers were regularly published and books were cheap and abundant. (4) The printing of visual material led to growing publishing practices; in the late eighteenth century, in the flourishing urban circles of Edo (Tokyo), illustrated collections of paintings depicted urban culture with its artists, courtesans and tea-house gatherings. (5) Books were also published on women, musical instruments, the tea ceremony, flower arrangement and proper etiquette.

items.stem:
How did the uses of print diversify in China by the 17th century ? Explain.
or
‘By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the use of print diversified.’ Give any three facts to support the statement.
or
How did a new reading culture bloom in China ? Explain.
items.answer: By the seventeenth century, as urban culture bloomed in China, the uses of print became far more varied. (1) Print was no longer confined to scholars and officials. (2) Merchants used print in their everyday work as they collected trade information, and reading turned into a leisure habit. (3) Rich women began to read, and many of them began publishing their poetry and plays. (4) The wives of scholar-officials published their works, and courtesans wrote about their own lives. Thus a new and much wider reading culture bloomed in China.

items.stem: How had the earliest printing technology developed in the world ? Explain.
items.answer: The earliest print technology grew up in East Asia. (1) It was developed in China, Japan and Korea. (2) Up to the sixth century print was used only by scholar-officials. (3) Buddhist monasteries then introduced hand-printing technology more widely. (4) Marco Polo carried woodblock printing from China to Italy. (5) From this beginning came the printing press, whose invention proved a great miracle in spreading knowledge.

items.stem: Give three methods by which printed books became more accessible to common people.
items.answer: Printed books reached common people through the following means. (1) The cost of producing books fell. (2) Books were printed in very large numbers. (3) Public libraries, book stalls and shops opened, lending or selling books at very little profit, and the habit of borrowing books from book banks made books still more accessible. (4) The spread of education, the spare time available to women at home and the desire to spend leisure in reading all widened the reading public.

items.stem: Why were the printed books popular even among illiterate people ?
items.answer: Printed books were popular even with those who could not read. (1) Common people lived in a world of oral culture in which sacred texts were read out, ballads recited and folk tales narrated, so knowledge reached illiterate people by ear. (2) Illiterate people heard a story collectively or saw a performance, and many were attracted by the beautiful pictures printed in the books. (3) Even those who could not read could enjoy listening to books being read out, so printers began publishing popular ballads and folk tales, profusely illustrated with pictures, which were then sung and recited at gatherings in villages and in taverns in towns.

items.stem: What do you understand by Print Revolution? How did the idea of the scientists and philosophers become more accessible to common man after beginning of this revolution in Europe ?
items.answer: The Print Revolution means the transformation brought about by modern printing technology, which covers not only printing but also the sizing and cutting of paper for the printed pages and the binding of those pages under a stiff or soft cover, so producing whole books, magazines and newspapers with or without illustrations. Before printing, and even in the early stage of woodblock printing, books could not be produced anywhere near as fast as they are today by rotary machines that print newspapers or by modern automatic electronic printers; printed material can now be ready for sale or distribution almost as soon as printing is complete. Because of this, the ideas of scientists such as Sir Isaac Newton, Einstein and Galileo, and of philosophers such as Thomas Paine, Voltaire and Jean Jacques Rousseau, could be read easily in books, so common people far beyond the authors' own circles benefited from their ideas, laws and rules, all fairly explained in print.

items.stem: Invention of printing press by Johann Gutenberg led to revolution in the realm of ideas. Justify.
items.answer: The Gutenberg Press was the breakthrough in print technology. It was at Strasbourg in Germany that Johann Gutenberg developed the first known printing press in the 1430s. He made metal types for each of the 26 characters of the Roman alphabet and devised a way of moving them about so as to compose different words of the text; this became the moveable type printing machine and remained the basic print technology for the next 300 years. Books could now be produced far faster than when each print block had to be carved out of wood by hand — the Gutenberg press could print 250 sheets on one side in an hour. The first book printed by Gutenberg was the Bible, and it took three years to print 180 copies. By multiplying books in this way the press spread ideas rapidly and so brought about a revolution in the realm of ideas.

items.stem: Why was there a strong criticism from some scholars against indiscriminate publication of all types of books ?
items.answer: Scholars feared print because it could not be controlled. (1) Their major fear was that if there was no control over what was printed and read, rebellious and irreligious thoughts might spread. (2) Priests, monks, bishops and the monarch regarded writers and artists as dangerous to their authority and influence over the people, since their own value would fall once things they alone knew became known to all. (3) An example from Europe is Manocchio, a miller in Italy, who acquired the ability to re-interpret the message of the Bible; he was warned twice and finally the inquisition (Trial Court) pronounced the death sentence against him. An Indian example is that many conservative Hindus and Muslims placed restrictions on the reading of books by women and by vulnerable sections of society, allowing only upper and middle class and caste people to read.
